questions.q: According to this lesson, what are the five things you need to know before you provision any real infrastructure?
options: Only the budget — everything else can be decided after deployment
The programming language the application is written in
The cloud provider's current stock price, uptime history, and marketing materials
Expected traffic/load, compliance requirements, budget constraints, availability needs, and who the users are
questions.explain: These five answers come from the stakeholder who owns the workload, not from a cloud console, and they drive every decision later in this chapter.

questions.q: Why does discovering a compliance requirement (like HIPAA) after a workload is already deployed cause expensive rework?
options: It doesn't cause any real problem — compliance can always be added instantly with no cost
Compliance requirements never change once a workload is deployed
Encryption, access logging, and network isolation have to be retrofitted onto a system that's already live, instead of designed in from the start
It only affects billing, never the architecture itself
questions.explain: Retrofitting controls onto a live system is far more expensive and disruptive than designing them in during planning.

questions.q: A team guesses at expected load instead of asking the stakeholder, and badly undersizes the infrastructure. What's the realistic consequence?
options: The workload becomes automatically compliant with HIPAA
Nothing — cloud infrastructure automatically fixes undersized guesses with no downtime
The monthly bill always ends up lower than expected
An outage the first time real traffic spikes, not just a minor slowdown
questions.explain: Undersized infrastructure chosen by guessing buckles under real load, which is an outage, not a convenience issue.

questions.q: Who should you actually ask to learn a workload's expected traffic, compliance needs, budget, and availability target?
options: The stakeholder who owns or requested the workload
No one — these should be inferred from the cloud console's default settings
The cloud provider's sales team, since they set these requirements
A random sample of end users, since their opinion overrides the business owner's
questions.explain: None of the five requirement categories require a cloud console — they require a direct conversation with the person who owns the workload.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a short written requirements brief matter beyond this single lesson?
options: It's discarded once the workload is deployed and never referenced again
It replaces the need for any architecture diagram later in the chapter
It's only useful for billing paperwork and has no bearing on technical decisions
It becomes the direct input used to choose a provider, size infrastructure, and design the architecture in the lessons that follow
questions.explain: Lesson 2 uses the brief to choose a provider, Lesson 3 uses it to size compute and storage, and Lesson 4 uses it to sketch the architecture.
